section_texts.abstract: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising technology that provides terabyte-scale accelerator-local capacity at bandwidths approaching HBM, with a potential cost-per-bit advan- tage over HBM. However, its NAND foundation brings long latency, out-of-place updates, and finite write endurance directly into the accelerator memory hierarchy, making its effects on performance and lifetime difficult to predict. To study this emerging design space, we present HBFSim, an LLM-aware event-driven simulator for het- erogeneous HBM+HBF memory systems that preserves application- level memory semantics while modeling flash-internal behavior. HBFSim models HBM, HBF with host-managed flash translation, and conventional capacity tiers in one simulation driven by a cal- ibrated serving frontend. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. HBF serves data that does not fit in HBM 11.0–19.0× faster than host DRAM; HBM is better used to hold the running sequences’ KV cache than as a cache for HBF; and at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B, HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes. The artifact is available at https://github.com/FlashLabAE/HBFSim and will track public HBF device data as it becomes available. section_texts.introduction: Memory capacity has emerged as a primary bottleneck in serv- ing large language models (LLMs). Model weights occupy tens to hundreds of gigabytes, while key–value (KV) state grows linearly with context length and request concurrency, quickly exceeding accelerator memory capacity. For example, an 8B model serving eight concurrent 128K-context sessions can exhaust the HBM of a modern GPU (e.g., the 131 GiB of HBM3e on an NVIDIA H200), while long-context serving for 70B-class models may exceed the memory capacity of an entire eight-GPU node [5, 11, 17, 22]. High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising ap- proach for extending accelerator-local memory capacity. SanDisk’s disclosed HBF design targets a 16-die, 512 GB flash stack that deliv- ers up to 1.6 TB/s [24, 25], enabling multi-terabyte accelerator-local memory systems without host-memory accesses. The same disclo- sure targets 8–16× HBM capacity at similar cost and bandwidth, making capacity per dollar, rather than higher speed, the main motivation for HBF [24]. Unlike conventional DRAM expansion, HBF brings asymmet- ric read and write performance, page programming, flash transla- tion layer (FTL) management, write amplification, and finite pro- gram/erase endurance into the accelerator memory hierarchy. Its effect on LLM serving is difficult to predict because no public HBF hardware is available for validation [28]. Nevertheless, system archi- tects must decide on memory organization, placement policies, and provisioning before production devices become available. For ex- ample, moving read-only weights to HBF mainly exercises its read arXiv:2610.23503v1 [cs.AR] 16 Oct 2026 RACS ’26, November 17–20, 2026, Fukuoka, Japan Li et al. Therefore, it is necessary to study the performance of HBM+HBF memory hierarchies under realistic LLM serving work- loads before committing to a design. Because such hardware is unavailable, a simulator is required to evaluate these trade-offs. Existing simulators each cover one level of this hierarchy: DRAM simulators [14, 16] stop at the memory controller, SSD simula- tors [13, 29] put flash behind a storage interface, and LLM serving simulators [4, 10, 36] represent memory by capacity and bandwidth. None connects the placement of LLM data to both completion time and physical flash traffic. HBFSim addresses this limitation. It models HBM, HBF with a host-managed FTL, and conventional capacity tiers in one event system, coupled in a closed loop with a serving frontend whose scheduler and GPU compute are calibrated against measurements, and it accepts address-level traces as well as production request traces. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. We find that HBF serves the data that does not fit in HBM 11.0–19.0× faster than host DRAM; that HBM should hold the running sequences’ KV, because caching HBF with LRU or FIFO rereads nearly the whole working set once it exceeds HBM, and that KV should be written to HBF only when it must leave HBM; and that the FTL costs little on the read path as long as its layout keeps reads parallel, while HBF’s lifetime depends on the amount of KV that reaches flash. These findings connect HBF’s potential cost-per-bit advantage to measurable latency and wear rather than to a single capacity or bandwidth number. This paper makes the following contributions: • Workloads at two granularities. HBFSim takes fine- grained address-level traces, with one record per memory access, and coarse-grained request traces, which its frontend expands into the series of weight and KV accesses that each request causes. • A coupled and fast memory-system model. HBM, HBF with a host-managed FTL, and external tiers (host DRAM, CXL SSDs, and NVMe SSDs) share one timeline and interact as in a real system, for example through the FTL’s tables in HBM. • Preliminary takeaways for HBF. Decoding Llama-3.1- 70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads yields five simple rules: HBF pays off only under capacity pressure; HBM should hold the running KV and HBF the weights, with KV written to flash only when it must leave HBM; generic cache replacement loses to this placement unless a step fits in HBM with room to spare; the FTL should preserve the flash array’s parallelism; and endurance, set by how much KV reaches flash, is a first-order constraint. 2.1 Memory Demand of LLM Serving A serving system’s memory holds the model weights, which every request reuses; the KV cache, the per-layer keys and values of every processed token, which decoding reads instead of recomputing; and activations, which are small by comparison. For Llama-3.1-70B a BF16 KV cache takes 320 KiB per token [5], 320 GiB for 1M tokens. Serving systems allocate KV in fixed-size blocks [11] and retain the blocks of finished requests so that later requests with the same prefix skip its prefill [22, 37], so the KV footprint grows beyond the active requests. Figure 1 shows the weights and the KV cache of 1M tokens, in one request or retained across many: for small models the KV cache dominates, every model from 70B up exceeds eight HBM4 stacks, and the newest open models, with 1.6T to 2.8T parameters, exceed even an eight-H200 node with their weights alone, while hybrid or compressed attention keeps their KV small. The two phases of a request access this data differently. Prefill processes the prompt, produces its KV, and is usually compute- bound; chunked prefill lets it share a batch with decoding work [2]. Each decoding step generates one token per request: it reuses the weights across the batch, reads every running request’s KV, and appends one token’s KV per layer, so it is usually bound by memory bandwidth, and its traffic grows with model size, batch, and context. When weights and KV exceed HBM, systems offload to host DRAM or SSDs [15, 22, 26], at access costs set by the slower tier and its interconnect. 2.2 High Bandwidth Flash HBF stacks NAND flash dies on a logic base die and connects them to the accelerator through an HBM-like interface in the same pack- age [24, 25]. The OCP HBF specification [19] defines stacks with up to 16 channels and three speed grades. For example, at speed grade 2 each channel carries 96 GB/s of payload, or about 1.5 TB/s per stack, and SanDisk targets 512 GB per stack. An HBF stack therefore offers 8-16 times the capacity of an HBM stack at a similar interface bandwidth. However, HBF still behaves like NAND. A page read takes mi- croseconds, compared to tens of nanoseconds of DRAM, so HBF reaches its bandwidth only with many reads in flight. Data is pro- grammed, not overwritten: a page program takes tens of microsec- onds and occupies its bank, and a block must be erased before its pages are programmed again. The specification assigns address mapping, garbage collection (GC), and wear leveling to host soft- ware; the device itself performs neither GC nor copyback [19]. Each block tolerates a limited number of program/erase (P/E) cycles, and no P/E rating for HBF has been published. Is HBF a better capacity tier than host DRAM or SSDs? How much HBM should accompany it? Which data should stay in HBM, and should HBM act as a cache for HBF or as sepa- rately addressed memory? How should the FTL handle KV writes? How long will HBF last under serving traffic? The answers depend on each other through the serving loop: slower memory stretches decoding steps, which changes how requests are batched and there- fore the memory traffic itself. Answering them requires running a real serving scheduler against memory models that include flash management, with the two coupled in a closed loop. HBFSIM DESIGN HBFSim is a closed-loop simulator of LLM serving on accelerator memory built from HBM, HBF, and other capacity tiers. Figure 2 shows its three layers. A serving frontend turns request traces into batches and the requests in each batch into memory accesses. A policy layer decides in which memory each object is stored and how data moves between tiers. A device engine executes the memory transactions on models of HBM, HBF, or external capacity tiers, and feeds the outcome of that work back to the frontend, which schedules the next batch based on the feedback. Slower memory therefore reshapes batching as it would on a real system: longer iterations let more requests queue before the next one starts, and when KV no longer fits, the scheduler moves some KV to a slower tier or preempts requests, which shrinks the batch. Three challenges shape this design. Workloads and device accesses differ in granularity and semantics. A serving system works with requests, weights, and KV blocks; HBM serves data bursts of tens of bytes; and HBF is accessed like memory but programs flash pages (e.g., 4 KiB) in order, erases whole flash blocks, and leaves its FTL to the host. Address-level traces preserve individual accesses but can only cover short runs, whereas production request traces cover long periods of serving but record no memory accesses. The levels of the memory hierarchy are coupled. Existing simulators model one level in isolation, but in an HBM+HBF sys- tem the two levels jointly determine performance. What HBF must serve depends on what HBM can hold, and the traffic HBF gener- ates in turn consumes HBM capacity and bandwidth. Placement decisions therefore shift load between the tiers rather than simply adding a slower level beneath HBM, so neither tier can be simulated independently. The number of events is huge. One decoding step of a 70B model reads tens of millions of flash pages, each passing through about a dozen shared resources, from the plane and flash channel to the TSVs and ECC engine. Because slower memory changes batching, these accesses must be simulated in a closed loop rather than replayed. As shown in Figure 2, layers in HBFSim communicate through narrow interfaces. The frontend describes work in terms of model objects such as weight tensors and KV blocks. Policies map objects to devices and emit transaction graphs with explicit dependencies. The engine contains no LLM-specific logic. This separation lets users change one layer, for example, add a caching policy or an FTL, without touching the others. 3.1 Serving Frontend HBFSim accepts workloads at two granularities. In an address-level trace, a record is one memory access with optional data class, ar- rival time, and layer annotations; such traces are replayed directly. Detailed instruction-and-address tracing and cycle-level simulation incur substantial costs even for a small inference workload. For Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (bfloat16, batch size 1), a 32-token prefill followed by two fixed-token decode steps required 43.4 minutes for trace collection on an RTX 4000 Ada with NVBit [30]. The resulting 1,030-kernel traces occupy 98.3 GiB uncompressed, or 7.46 GiB in the compressed format consumed by Accel-Sim2.0 [20]. Full trace- driven simulation already takes 19.9 wall-clock hours even for a small model. For larger models, both the trace size and simulation time would become prohibitively large, rendering this approach unrealistic. In a request-level trace, a record is one inference request: its arrival time, prompt and output lengths, and prefix hashes [22, 31]. It contains no detailed memory accesses. Which bytes an inference step touches does not depend on the values it computes, only on the model architecture and on which requests the scheduler runs with how many tokens (for MoE models, also on the routed experts, which depend on the values and are therefore an input, recorded or synthetic). The frontend, ServeLoop, therefore regenerates the accesses of every step. Its scheduler replays the trace with vLLM’s continuous batching and chunked prefill [2, 11, 35], including paged KV, prefix sharing, and preemption. A compiler turns each iteration into the byte ranges that every operator reads or writes in weight tensors, KV blocks, and embedding rows, leaving addresses and memories to the policies. A decoding step of Llama-3.1-70B under the workload with 32 sequences and 6K tokens of context becomes 1.8 × 105 such transactions. The generated accesses are verified at three levels. Batching: given the same service times, the scheduler forms the same batches RACS ’26, November 17–20, 2026, Fukuoka, Japan Li et al. as vLLM (Section 3.5). Addresses: the byte ranges and their order match 6,568 held-out warp streams captured with NVBit on an A100; the H200 we model has no capture, so its KV is read block by block, which changes the time per output token (TPOT) by at most 0.55% against the A100 order. Volume: the frontend counts each byte once, whereas prefill kernels refetch the same KV for other query heads or tiles, which GPU caches partly absorb, so prefill traffic is a lower bound. HBFSim times every batch, prefill and decode alike, using an operator-level GPU model. It decomposes each batch into opera- tors and computes each operator’s time from three components: a fixed overhead, a compute time, and a memory-access time. The compute time is derived from the operator’s FLOPs and a compute- throughput coefficient fitted to measured kernels. We obtain the memory-access time from HBFSim’s detailed simulation of HBM and HBF accesses, rather than an ideal-bandwidth assumption. To stay anchored to real GPU behavior, we fit each operator’s fixed overhead, compute throughput, and memory bandwidth from mea- sured kernels to establish a baseline time. During simulation, we replace the baseline’s ideal memory time with the simulated access time, while retaining the measured kernel’s additional memory overhead beyond the GPU’s peak bandwidth. The batch time is then the sum of all operator times. This design ensures that HBF latency and bandwidth directly affect each operator’s memory time, and thus the batch time, while the compute portion stays tied to measured GPU performance. 3.2 Memory Policies HBFSim provides two ways to organize HBM and HBF. In peer mode, HBM and HBF form one address space, and each object is stored in one of them. HBM is filled in a priority order and the rest overflows to HBF: weights first places the weights, then KV blocks in address order, retained prefixes included; KV first places the running sequences’ KV, then the weights, then the retained prefixes. In tiered mode, HBM caches objects stored in the HBF or other capacity tier in 4 MiB lines with LRU, FIFO, or decayed-LFU [23] replacement; decayed LFU evicts the line with the fewest recent accesses and halves all access counts periodically, as in frequency- based replacement [23]. Dirty data is tracked at 4 KiB granularity, and dirty KV is written back either eagerly, while compute leaves the link idle [12], or only when its line is evicted. KV released before eviction is discarded without being written. 3.3 Device Engine HBM. An HBM stack follows the JEDEC organization of its gen- eration, set by the number of channels and pseudo-channels and the pin rate. The following study uses HBM4 for analysis [8], with 32 channels of two pseudo-channels at 8 Gb/s per pin, or 2 TB/s per stack. Because our studies concern capacity tiers, HBFSim mod- els HBM at the pseudo-channel level rather than at the command level of DRAM simulators such as Ramulator 2.0 [16]. Requests are split into pseudo-channel transfers, groups of four pseudo-channels share an arbitration queue and a service timeline, and an average ac- cess latency and a bandwidth efficiency account for row activation and refresh. HBF. As in the OCP specification, the model separates the device from its host-side management. The device has independent trans- mit and receive timelines for each channel, ordered page sensing within each bank, page buffers, ECC, and TSV transfers. It programs the pages of a block in order and, as the specification requires, erases a block when its first page is written. The organization of flash into channels, dies, planes, and blocks and the timing of reads, programs, and erases follow MQSim [29]. We reimplemented them because MQSim’s FTL runs inside an SSD, whereas HBF’s runs on the host, and HBF operations must share one timeline with HBM and the serving frontend. Like an SSD, and beyond the specification, each stack has a device-managed DRAM that buffers writes until a page is full and caches recently read pages. The host runs the FTL. It maps logical pages to physical ones and runs garbage collection, which picks victim blocks by their number of valid pages with a small weight for wear; static wear leveling is implemented but switched off in our studies. Since the specification forbids the device from moving valid data, garbage collection reads live pages into a copy buffer in HBM and writes them back. We implemented three mappings and keep each one’s index in HBM. Page-level mapping has an 8-byte entry per 4 KiB page; the whole table lives in flash as translation pages, and HBM caches part of it. Extent mapping keeps a sorted list of runs of consecutive pages, 48 B per run. Both write by appending and spread consecutive pages over all planes. Block- level mapping has one entry per 1 MiB logical block and keeps the block in one physical block on one plane, each page at a fixed offset. We model two consequences: NAND programs a block’s pages in order, so a page whose predecessors have not been written yet waits in the device DRAM; and any write that is not an in-order append copies the whole block to a fresh one. We do not stripe blocks over planes, because a copy would then move a 1.5 GiB stripe. Every mapping gets 0.1% of the HBF capacity in HBM, 3.1 GiB of the 96 GiB of two HBM4 stacks, and its lookups compete with the application’s traffic: with page-level mapping, one Llama-3.1-70B decoding step at 2 HBM + 6 HBF issues 1.0–1.7×107 lookups, one per flash page read. Other tiers. Host DRAM, CXL SSDs, and NVMe SSDs share one model consisting of a link, a controller, and media queues. A CXL SSD adds a device-side DRAM cache with FIFO replacement. 3.4 Simulation Speed To make full-iteration simulation tractable, we combine coarse- grained HBM approximation with exact HBF acceleration. Only HBM is approximated: scheduling transfers per 4 KiB chunk and pseudo-channel rather than per 32-byte burst runs an all-HBM for- ward pass 24.8× faster (134.7× for sequential reads), while keeping batch completion times within 0.04%. For HBF, the bottleneck is reserving roughly a dozen shared resources per page, as in SimpleSSD [9]; here we reduce per- reservation overhead without sacrificing accuracy. A first-fit calen- dar organizes each resource’s idle intervals into 64-interval leaves labeled with their maximum duration, so searches immediately bypass leaves with insufficient space. The HBF specification is still a draft, so we ask which device pa- rameters the results depend on, taking Llama-3.1-70B on the three workloads at 2 HBM + 6 HBF with KV first, where a step reads 29–49 GiB of weights from HBF (69–83 ms per token), and changing one parameter at a time (Figure 9). Ramulator 2.0 [16] and DRAMsim3 [14] model DRAM at the command level. MQSim [29] and FEMU [13] model SSDs behind an NVMe interface, with map- ping, GC, and wear leveling inside the device, and Cylon [34] emu- lates CXL SSDs with a DRAM cache in the device. HBFSim follows MQSim’s approach to the flash organization and Cylon’s device class for the CXL SSD, but treats HBF as memory with a host-side FTL whose metadata competes with the application in HBM. LLM serving simulators. Vidur [1], LLMServingSim [3], Fron- tier [6], and ASTRA-sim [33] simulate scheduling, computation, and communication for LLM inference, LLMCompass [36] adds operator-level modeling with mapping search, and GTSim [4] and Accel-Sim [10, 20] model GPU microarchitecture. abstract.text: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising technology that provides terabyte-scale accelerator-local capacity at bandwidths approaching HBM, with a potential cost-per-bit advan- tage over HBM. However, its NAND foundation brings long latency, out-of-place updates, and finite write endurance directly into the accelerator memory hierarchy, making its effects on performance and lifetime difficult to predict.

To study this emerging design space, we present HBFSim, an LLM-aware event-driven simulator for het- erogeneous HBM+HBF memory systems that preserves application- level memory semantics while modeling flash-internal behavior. HBFSim models HBM, HBF with host-managed flash translation, and conventional capacity tiers in one simulation driven by a cal- ibrated serving frontend.

Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. HBF serves data that does not fit in HBM 11.0–19.0× faster than host DRAM; HBM is better used to hold the running sequences’ KV cache than as a cache for HBF; and at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B, HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes.

The artifact is available at https://github.com/FlashLabAE/HBFSim and will track public HBF device data as it becomes available. CCS CONCEPTS • Computing methodologies →Simulation tools; • Computer systems organization →Heterogeneous (hybrid) systems; • Infor- mation systems →Flash memory.

introduction.text: Memory capacity has emerged as a primary bottleneck in serv- ing large language models (LLMs). Model weights occupy tens to hundreds of gigabytes, while key–value (KV) state grows linearly with context length and request concurrency, quickly exceeding accelerator memory capacity.

For example, an 8B model serving eight concurrent 128K-context sessions can exhaust the HBM of a modern GPU (e.g., the 131 GiB of HBM3e on an NVIDIA H200), while long-context serving for 70B-class models may exceed the memory capacity of an entire eight-GPU node [5, 11, 17, 22]. High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising ap- proach for extending accelerator-local memory capacity.

SanDisk’s disclosed HBF design targets a 16-die, 512 GB flash stack that deliv- ers up to 1.6 TB/s [24, 25], enabling multi-terabyte accelerator-local memory systems without host-memory accesses. The same disclo- sure targets 8–16× HBM capacity at similar cost and bandwidth, making capacity per dollar, rather than higher speed, the main motivation for HBF [24].

Unlike conventional DRAM expansion, HBF brings asymmet- ric read and write performance, page programming, flash transla- tion layer (FTL) management, write amplification, and finite pro- gram/erase endurance into the accelerator memory hierarchy. Its effect on LLM serving is difficult to predict because no public HBF hardware is available for validation [28].

Nevertheless, system archi- tects must decide on memory organization, placement policies, and provisioning before production devices become available. Therefore, it is necessary to study the performance of HBM+HBF memory hierarchies under realistic LLM serving work- loads before committing to a design. Because such hardware is unavailable, a simulator is required to evaluate these trade-offs.

Existing simulators each cover one level of this hierarchy: DRAM simulators [14, 16] stop at the memory controller, SSD simula- tors [13, 29] put flash behind a storage interface, and LLM serving simulators [4, 10, 36] represent memory by capacity and bandwidth. None connects the placement of LLM data to both completion time and physical flash traffic.

HBFSim addresses this limitation. It models HBM, HBF with a host-managed FTL, and conventional capacity tiers in one event system, coupled in a closed loop with a serving frontend whose scheduler and GPU compute are calibrated against measurements, and it accepts address-level traces as well as production request traces.

Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. These findings connect HBF’s potential cost-per-bit advantage to measurable latency and wear rather than to a single capacity or bandwidth number. This paper makes the following contributions: • Workloads at two granularities.

HBFSim takes fine- grained address-level traces, with one record per memory access, and coarse-grained request traces, which its frontend expands into the series of weight and KV accesses that each request causes. • A coupled and fast memory-system model.
